lead: Linked lists, trees and graphs store data in separate node objects joined by references. The references replace the contiguous block that a Python list needs. A linked list follows one next pointer; a binary tree follows left and right pointers; a graph follows an adjacency list of neighbours. These structures let size grow without shifting elements, and they model trains, folders, road maps and social networks. Only a few universities teach this advanced material. Some syllabi call this linked structures or non-linear data structures.
prereq: You need: recursion from Unit 2; classes and objects from Unit 4; and list indexing from Unit 3.

sections.h3: Singly linked list: data and next

blocks.text: A singly linked list stores each item in a Node object. The object has data and next. The head reference points to the first node. The last node has next = None. There is no index; you walk from the head. This avoids shifting all later items when the list grows.

items: Traverse: start at head; read data; move to node.next; stop at None.
Insert at head: create a node; set new.next = head; set head = new.
Delete head: if head is not None, set head = head.next.
Append at tail: create a node. If the list is empty, set head = new; otherwise walk to the last node and set last.next = new. Keeping a tail reference makes append O(1).

blocks.text: In Python, define __init__(self, data) to set self.data = data and self.next = None. Appending 10, 20, 30 gives 10 → 20 → 30. Deleting the head updates head to the 20 node; the old 10 node is no longer reachable. Insert and delete at head cost O(1); traversal costs O(n). The None stop is essential; without it the walk never ends. The same pattern supports a stack.

sections.h3: Binary tree and binary search tree

blocks.text: A binary tree node holds data, left and right. The top node is the root. A binary search tree (BST) adds one rule: for every node, all keys in its left subtree are smaller, and all keys in its right subtree are larger.

items: Insert key: if the subtree is empty, return a new node. Compare key with current data. Go left if smaller, right if larger. Repeat; attach the new node at the empty slot.
Search key: compare at the root. Go left if key is smaller, right if larger. Stop at the key or at None.

blocks.text: Traversals list nodes. Inorder visits left subtree, node, right subtree. Preorder visits node, left, right. Postorder visits left, right, node. In a valid BST, inorder gives sorted keys. Define height as the number of edges on the longest root-to-leaf path. Worst-case search takes height + 1 comparisons. A skewed tree of n nodes has height n−1.

A graph has vertices and edges. An adjacency list maps each vertex to a list of neighbours. For an undirected edge, add both directions. For a directed edge, add one direction. Each edge appears twice in an undirected adjacency list.

Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a queue. Put the start in the queue and mark it visited. Repeat: remove a vertex; for each unvisited neighbour, mark it and add it to the queue. Depth-first search (DFS) uses a stack or recursion: mark a vertex, then go deep into one unvisited neighbour before returning.

The visited set is required: without it, a cycle sends the traversal round forever. Use a set for visited because membership is average O(1). BFS finds shortest edge-count paths in an unweighted graph. For a Chennai road map, vertices are junctions and edges are roads.

figure.caption: The binary search tree after inserting 50, 30, 70, 20, 40. Inorder reads 20, 30, 40, 50, 70; searching 40 compares 50, then 30, then 40.

spec.aria: A binary search tree with root 50, left child 30 with children 20 and 40, and right child 70; inorder gives 20, 30, 40, 50, 70.

examples.question: Insert 50, 30, 70, 20, 40 into an empty binary search tree in that order. Draw the tree, give the inorder traversal, and search for 40: list the nodes compared. Then build a singly linked list by appending 10, 20, 30 and give the list after deleting the head.
steps: Search 40: compare 50, go left; compare 30, go right; compare 40, found. Three comparisons.
examples.answer: Inorder is 20, 30, 40, 50, 70; search compares 50, 30, 40 (3 comparisons); after head deletion the list is 20 → 30.

traps: A BST inorder traversal is sorted only if the BST rule holds at every node.
A graph traversal needs a visited set to avoid cycles.
Deleting a linked-list head must update the head reference.
In a BST search, compare before moving; do not move first.

quiz.q: In a singly linked list, what two attributes does a Node hold?
Why does a graph traversal need a visited set?
quiz.a: To stop revisiting vertices and to terminate on cycles.

quiz.q: In the BST from the example, where is 35 inserted?
quiz.a: 35 < 50: go left; 35 > 30: go right; 35 < 40: insert as left child of 40.

quiz.q: After deleting the head of 10 → 20 → 30, what is the list?
Why can a sorted Python list not replace a linked list when you insert at the head often?
quiz.a: List insert at head shifts n items; linked-list head insert is O(1).

quiz.q: Name the three depth-first traversal orders of a binary tree.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real systems use balanced trees such as B-trees in databases to keep height small. Graphs drive maps, package managers and social feeds; BFS and DFS are the base for later shortest-path work. Search for AVL tree, Dijkstra's algorithm and adjacency matrix next.
